title: Beyond the Binary: Duality, Non-Duality and the Semitic Third Space
subtitle: Why so many traditions say that two is not the last word: the One, the mirror of the pair, and the third space between.
summary: We see the world in pairs: light and dark, self and other. The contemplative traditions say duality is real but not ultimate. How Arabic grammar treats two as neither one nor many, three parables that see through surface opposites, the two ways of divine love, and practices for living rooted in the One.
aiNote: Rough draft for review: the Verses Across team's own essay, edited and fact-checked with AI. Scripture is quoted from the public-domain translations on this site (King James Version, Pickthall's Qur'an, Legge's Tao Te Ching).

medium.html:
"The Tao produced One; One produced Two; Two produced Three; Three produced All things. All things leave behind them the Obscurity (out of which they have come), and go forward to embrace the Brightness (into which they have emerged), while they are harmonised by the Breath of Vacancy." (Tao Te Ching 42)

To be human is to wake up in a world of apparent opposites. From our first breath, perception divides reality into light and shadow, self and other, subject and object, sacred and ordinary. In Advaita Vedanta, the Hindu philosophy of non-duality, this shimmering web of opposites is called maya: the creative illusion that shows the one Ground of Being as a fractured world of many things. Western philosophy and theology describe a comparable condition as the fallen, divided state of creatures.

Yet across the great contemplative traditions, from Hindu Advaita to Taoist harmony, from the Kabbalah's Ein Sof to Islamic tawhid and Christian mysticism, one bold claim keeps returning: duality is not the final truth about reality. It is a lens in between, through which the Infinite shows and mirrors itself.

This essay explores duality and non-duality through language, metaphysics, scripture and devotion. In particular, it looks at something built into classical Arabic: two is not a plural. The pair is a mirror, a third space between the undivided One and the endless Many.

Before there were two: is God above duality or within it?

Before asking how to go beyond duality, we can ask what came before it, and where the Divine stands in relation to it.

Across traditions, ultimate reality in its unmanifest state is described as absolute, unconditioned unity: Advaita's nirguna Brahman (reality without attributes, from the Upanishads), Taoism's unnameable Tao, the Kabbalah's Ein Sof (the Endless), Islam's al-Ahad (the One). In that state there is no subject watching an object; no distance, no time, no collision, no shadow.

Above duality, and within it

Is God above duality or within it? The mystical traditions answer: both, and bound by neither. In the divine essence (dhat in Islamic thought, nirguna in Hindu), God is utterly beyond duality: beyond light and dark, beyond creator and created. Yet through self-manifestation (tajalli, saguna), God enters duality, the hidden life within every pair of opposites. On this view, duality does not exist beside God as a second reality; it is the veil of divine light.

Chapter 42 of the Tao Te Ching describes creation as an unfolding of numbers: from the nameless comes the One; from the One, the Two (yin and yang, heaven and earth); from the Two, the Three (their living harmony); and from the Three, all things. Duality is not an accident or a mistake, but the stage through which the One mirrors itself.

How language shapes duality: Western pairs and the Semitic three

The way a language is built may reflect, and shape, how its speakers picture reality, and here a striking contrast appears.

The Western split

In the European languages, the words for two (Latin duo, Greek dyo, English two) gather associations of division and conflict. From the same root come doubt (Latin dubitare, a mind split two ways) and duplicity (being double-faced); duel has long been linked with them too, though it really comes from an old Latin word for war. The devil belongs to the same family of ideas by meaning rather than by root: Greek diabolos comes from dia-ballein, "to throw across", and means the slanderer, the one who sets people against each other.

Sanskrit and ancient Greek still had a third grammatical number, the dual, for pairs. But modern English and most modern European languages have lost it. In them, reality is a flat either-or: one or many, singular or plural, subject or object, with no form of its own for two.

The Semitic three: the third space built into Arabic

Classical Arabic kept the dual, and still uses it. Its grammar has three numbers, not two, and two is not a plural. Plural (jam') begins at three.

  • The singular (mufrad): one. Unity, the undivided individual; in theology, tawhid, the oneness of God.
  • The dual (muthanna): two. A pair in balance, in tension, mirroring each other: not a crowd, but a mirror and a bridge.
  • The plural (jam'): three or more. True multiplicity: community, a collection, the countless things of creation.

The dual matters. Because two is not a plural, a pair is treated as a relationship, a mirror, rather than a scattering. The dual is a threshold between absolute oneness and endless multiplicity. (Biblical Hebrew keeps a dual too, mostly for natural pairs: hands, eyes, ears, feet.)

The barzakh: the third space in Islamic thought

In the Sufi metaphysics of Ibn Arabi, this grammar has a cosmic counterpart: the barzakh, the isthmus or in-between realm. A barzakh stands between two realities, like the line between sunlight and shadow, or the world of imagination between pure spirit and matter. It belongs fully to neither side, yet joins both. It keeps opposites from collapsing into war or splitting apart forever.

Three parables that see through the veil of opposites

Prophets and sages use parables to expose the limits of surface, either-or thinking. Three of them, from the Gospels, Hindu philosophy and the Qur'an, show the move from seeing in pairs to seeing whole.

Cleaning the cup (Matthew 23:25–26)

Jesus rebukes the Pharisees: "Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye make clean the outside of the cup and of the platter, but within they are full of extortion and excess. Thou blind Pharisee, cleanse first that which is within the cup and platter, that the outside of them may be clean also." (Matthew 23:25–26)

This is more than a warning against hypocrisy. It challenges a split way of seeing religion: outside against inside, ritual purity treated as something separate from a changed heart. Jesus shows that inside and outside are one continuous surface. When the inner eye is made clean, outward action follows naturally, without performance.

The rope and the snake (Advaita Vedanta)

In the teaching of Adi Shankara, a traveler walks a dusty road at dusk. Suddenly he sees a coiled snake in his path. His heart races and he freezes in fear. Then someone brings a lamp, and he sees that the "snake" was only a coil of old rope.

**Superimposition (adhyasa).** The traveler's fear was real, but the snake never existed. It was laid over the rope by dim light: ignorance (avidya). In the same way, Advaita teaches, the separate ego, fear, death and division are laid over the one rope of pure Consciousness, Brahman. Liberation (moksha) does not mean killing the snake. It means lighting the lamp, and seeing that there was only ever the rope.

Moses and al-Khidr (Qur'an 18:60–82)

In the Qur'an's eighteenth surah, Moses seeks out a mysterious servant of God, known in tradition as al-Khidr, "the Green One". God says of him that We "had taught him knowledge from Our presence" (Qur'an 18:65). Moses asks to follow and learn, and is warned: "Lo! thou canst not bear with me. How canst thou bear with that whereof thou canst not compass any knowledge?" (Qur'an 18:67–68)

On their journey Khidr does three shocking things:

  • He makes a hole in the boat they are sailing in (Qur'an 18:71).
  • He kills a lad they meet on the way (Qur'an 18:74).
  • He repairs a falling wall in a town that had refused them food (Qur'an 18:77).

Each time Moses judges by the surface: good or evil, lawful or unlawful. Before they part, Khidr reveals what lay beneath. The boat "belonged to poor people working on the river, and I wished to mar it, for there was a king behind them who is taking every ship by force" (Qur'an 18:79). The lad's parents were believers, and Khidr feared he would oppress them "by rebellion and disbelief" (Qur'an 18:80). And beneath the wall lay a treasure belonging to two orphan boys, kept "as a mercy from their Lord" until they came of age (Qur'an 18:82). What Moses saw as three disasters were, seen whole, three mercies. Khidr stands for the vision that looks past surface judgment to the hidden wholeness of God's plan.

The paradox of love: devotion in two and in one

One of the deepest questions in the spiritual life is about love: does love need two?

Love across the distance (bhakti, I and Thou)

In paths of devotion, such as Hindu bhakti and most Jewish, Christian and Muslim worship, love depends on the difference between lover and Beloved, the worshipper and God: in Martin Buber's words, I and Thou. The Bengali mystic Ramakrishna, a devotee of the goddess Kali, loved a saying of the poet Ramprasad: he wanted to taste sugar, not to become sugar.

Here the distance between Creator and creature is kept as holy ground, the space across which longing, praise, tears and devotion can flow. Love is a bridge between two shores.

Love as the ocean (Advaita and Sufi fana)

In non-dual paths, such as the jnana of Advaita or the Sufi fana (passing away of the self), the distinction is seen as scaffolding. Love is not a link between two separate things; it is the discovery that the separation was never final.

In Sufi poetry the lover enters the fire of devotion until the lover burns away and only Love remains. The pair, lover and Beloved, resolves into the One. The soul finds that God was not an object across the room to be praised, but the very Subject looking out through its eyes. The Christian mystic Meister Eckhart put it this way in a sermon: "The eye through which I see God is the same eye through which God sees me; my eye and God's eye are one eye, one seeing, one knowing, one love."

Practices for seeing whole

How do we loosen the grip of either-or seeing in daily life? Liberation, moksha, fana or awakening, is not an escape from the world into a void. It is a change of sight that sees unity within a world of opposites.

Self-inquiry (atma-vichara)

Taught by Ramana Maharshi, this practice turns the mind back to its source. Whenever a thought arises ("I am anxious", "he is wrong", "I lack this"), ask: "To whom does this thought arise?" The answer is "to me." Then the decisive question: "Who am I?" Followed back past thoughts, feelings and sensations, the sense of "I" opens into the quiet, boundless awareness beneath all experience.

Silent prayer and remembrance (Hesychasm and dhikr)

In Eastern Christian Hesychasm, the Jesus Prayer is repeated in rhythm with the breath and heartbeat; in Sufi dhikr, the remembrance of God is repeated in the same way. Sacred repetition quiets the restless, judging mind. As judgments fade, the heart enters the third space of silent presence, where the one who prays and the One who hears draw near beyond words.

Awareness without grasping (Vipassana and Zen)

In Buddhist insight meditation and in Zen, freedom grows by watching opposites arise and pass (pleasure and pain, heat and cold, praise and blame) without taking sides or clinging to either. When we stop labeling every experience "good" or "bad", the tension that feeds suffering loosens.

Living in the world, rooted in the One

Our age suffers from a sickness of the binary. Politics, media and technology push people into rigid camps: us against them, right against wrong, zero against one. The result is endless conflict.

The old wisdom of non-duality and the Semitic third space offers medicine for our time:

  • Honor the pair without idolizing it. We can accept the great pairs (male and female, work and rest, light and shade) as beautiful, necessary mirrors, without mistaking them for ultimate reality.
  • Step into the third space. In conflict, we can refuse flat either-or choices and look for the deeper meeting point that reconciles opposites.
  • Stay anchored in the One. Through daily silence, prayer and unattached awareness, we can stay rooted in a peace deeper than opposites while moving through the dance of everyday life.

May we see past the veil of maya and the illusion of a divided world, and discover that behind every mirror, beneath every shadow and within every heart, there has only ever been the One.

Reflection

  • Where in your life are you stuck in an either-or that might have a third way?
  • Have you ever, like Moses with Khidr, judged something as bad that later proved to be a mercy?
  • Does your prayer or meditation feel more like love across a distance, or like coming home to the One?
